Get started with BLASTr

Source: vignettes/BLASTr.qmd

BLASTr searches many sequences with BLAST+ from R and returns the hits ranked, a summary per sequence and the consensus lowest common ancestor of the best hits, with the NCBI taxonomy. This vignette goes from a FASTA file to a summary per sequence, with the small database that comes with the package. It runs in a few seconds and needs no internet.

library(BLASTr)

Install

BLASTr is installed from GitHub; BLAST+ 2.17.0 is installed by install_dependencies() in a conda environment of its own (blastr-blast-env), through the condathis package. Without it, BLASTr uses the BLAST+ of the system, if it is 2.16.0 or newer.

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("heronoh/BLASTr")
BLASTr::install_dependencies()

The code below runs only where BLAST+ is ready (has_blast()).

blast_ready <- has_blast()
blast_ready
#> [1] FALSE

A BLAST database from a FASTA file

make_blast_db() formats a FASTA file as a BLAST database. The package has a small one, minimal_db_blast.fasta, with 47 GenBank sequences. For real analyses, download_blast_db() downloads any database of the NCBI (such as core_nt) with the taxonomy of the same date, and make_unite_db() and make_silva_db() build UNITE and SILVA as BLAST databases (see their help pages).

fasta <- system.file("extdata", "minimal_db_blast.fasta", package = "BLASTr")
db <- file.path(tempdir(), "minimal_db_blast")
make_blast_db(fasta, db_path = db)

Searching

parallel_blast() takes a character vector of sequences and the path of the database. It chooses how to split the search (how many blastn processes, threads per process and sequences per batch) from the size of the database and the cores (total_cores) and RAM available; blast_strategy() shows the choice before the search.

seqs <- readLines(system.file("extdata", "seqs_test.txt", package = "BLASTr"))
length(seqs)
blast_strategy(n_seqs = length(seqs), db_path = db, total_cores = 2)
res <- parallel_blast(seqs, db, total_cores = 2)

By default, BLAST keeps up to 100 subjects per sequence (search_alignments) with at least 80% identity (perc_id) and 50% query coverage (search_qcov_hsp).

Reading the results

The result has one row per hit, best first, and one row with empty hit fields for each sequence without hits:

res[, c("Sequence", "rank", "tie", "at_best", "subject", "identity", "qcovhsp", "Similarity score", "low_qcov")]
  • Similarity score is (10 * identity + qcovhsp) / 11 (see similarity_score()). The hits are ranked by it (rank_by = "similarity"), then by identity, coverage, bitscore and BLAST order. blast_rank keeps the order of BLAST, which favours longer alignments.
  • at_best marks the hits within check_tolerance (0.5 points) of the best one: the tied candidates for the identification. tie marks hits with the same value as another one.
  • low_qcov marks hits that cover less than perc_qcov_hsp (80%) of the sequence; they are kept and ranked, but the identification of a sequence whose best hit has low_qcov rests on a partial alignment.
  • informative is FALSE for references that do not inform the identification (uncultured, environmental, metagenomes, vectors…; see uninformative_references()); they get no rank and come after the informative hits.
  • The first 10 ranked hits (num_alignments) are kept, plus all the hits at best.

One row per sequence

blast_summary() summarises the hits of each sequence:

blast_summary(res)

Check ID is "best ID" when all the hits at best among the first 10 have the taxid of the first hit, and "check ID" otherwise (another taxid, or an unknown one, as here: the example database has no taxids). At best truncated is TRUE when the last subject BLAST returned is tied with the best one, so more tied subjects may exist beyond search_alignments.

Taxonomy and the lowest common ancestor

With a database that has taxids (download_blast_db(), make_unite_db(), make_silva_db(), or make_blast_db(taxid_map = )), get_tax() adds the NCBI taxonomy of each taxid from a local SQLite database (it comes with download_blast_db(); otherwise get_tax(res, download = TRUE) downloads the NCBI taxdump of the date of the BLAST database once), and blast_lca() gives the deepest taxon that contains at least 90% of the hits tied with the best one:

tax <- get_tax(res)
dplyr::left_join(res, tax, by = c(staxid = "taxid"))
lca <- blast_lca(res)

The help pages of get_tax() and blast_lca() have examples that run with a small taxonomy written on the spot.
